Initially the archivist reads it as a message from her future self warning her, a paradox, a ghost. The salt came back overnight. It always did. Nell took the phone from the biscuit tin, turned it until the window light caught the charging port, and worked a wooden toothpick along the seam. A fine white crust gave way in grits onto the tray. For the wider bloom across the back case she used a toothbrush gone soft with use, and kept the cotton buds in a jam jar with the label peeled off. Three phones and a dictaphone waited in the tin, each with a strip of masking tape and a number in pencil. Nineteen had been the worst. She could hear the crystals crunch as the connector went in, a small sound like a biscuit breaking.

The council had issued her a dehumidifier rated for a room half this size, which she supposed was forward planning.

It had been the library reading room. Now the shelves held card boxes and a row of labelled drives, and the radiator had been taken out to make way for the dehumidifier's tube, which ran through a hole in the skirting and dripped into a bucket. Through the tall windows she could read the numbers painted on the kerbs opposite — 12, 14, 16 — white still, put there for the crews. The houses behind them were empty. The removal vans had stopped in September. At spring tides the water came up into the car park and sat for an hour, as if considering, then went back down.

The council called it the Record of Leaving. The printed brief said *oral materials of the retiring community*. In practice people handed her devices: old phones, an answering machine, a child's recorder shaped like a whale, a tablet with a cracked corner. Inside each, buried among photographs and expired voicemail, were voice memos that had been recorded and never sent. Drafts. Rehearsals. She catalogued them on cards — owner, device, date, duration — and in the last column wrote the word *unsent*. She had written it two hundred and eleven times.

A man from Fennel Lane had recorded an apology to a brother up north seven times, each shorter than the one before; the seventh was four seconds and a click. A woman had sung two lines to a daughter who had not come to the door in six years, then said "No," and stopped the file. A child had recorded the sea for three minutes and named it *for later*. Nell never trimmed the silence at the end of a recording. She kept it. It seemed to her the truest part, the few seconds after a person had decided not to say any more.

Salt kept things and salt ate things, and she had never been able to separate the two. It drew the damp out of a circuit board and left a white map across the contacts; it fogged the inside of a screen until a face looked out through gauze; it crept beneath the glass of the drive caddies and made a faint tidemark along the rim. Every morning she cleaned what she had cleaned the day before. The bucket under the skirting filled with water that smelled of the cellar. In the afternoons, when the light went flat, the drives ticked in the rack like something cooling.

One device had no number. It had been on the desk the first morning, before she was given the key: a small silver recorder in a padded envelope, no note, the flap gone tacky with damp. She had written *22* on a strip of tape herself, put it at the bottom of the tin, and kept not reaching it.

When she finally connected it, the port was clean — the only clean one she had had — and the single file came across with its metadata intact. The date field read 04.11.36. Her log lay open beside her at 04.11.26. She checked the date on the recorder, then the wall calendar, then the phone in her pocket, though none of them had anything to do with the number in the field. The waveform was nine seconds long. She put the headphones on.

"Don't send it," her own voice said. Then a breath, and the small catch at the back of the throat she had heard all her life on the few recordings anyone had ever made of her. "It was never for anyone."

The voice was hers, gone slightly rough, the vowels worn narrow the way voices do when they have been used less. Ten years of it sat in the space between the two sentences. She took off the headphones. The room went on ticking.

She played it four times. Between the third and the fourth she got up and wiped the contacts of a phone she had already cleaned, though there was nothing on them. She did not write a card. She did not put it with the others. She copied it onto a drive of its own and carried it in her coat pocket, where it made a small hard square against her hip all afternoon.

On her own phone there was a memo eleven seconds long, recorded six times, which she had never sent and never deleted. Her sister rang on Sunday evenings from the new estate above the bypass, and they talked about the roof, the road, the forms. Afterwards Nell would open the memo, listen to the first second, and close it again. She set the phone face down on the table.

By the end of the week she had decided, without deciding, that it was a warning. There was a last transfer to make on Friday: the whole catalogue going up the line to the county server before the exchange closed and the road was given back. She had the upload queued and kept finding reasons not to plug the drive in. It sounded like somebody ten years older who knew how the whole thing turned out and had called back to save her the trouble — who knew that no one would ever open the files, that two hundred and eleven people saying nothing to nobody had been a waste of a winter. She heard it in the van, in the dehumidifier's click, in the pause before the kettle boiled. It was the first thing anyone had told her in months that she could not put on a card.

Number 14 had kept its curtains. On the Thursday before the exchange closed, Mr. Coyle came in with a biscuit tin of his own and set it on the desk, keeping his hand on the lid. "She made them after I'd gone up," he said. "I could hear her from the front room. Never loud." He looked at the rack of drives. "Will they go to anyone?"

"They'll be kept," Nell said. It was the only true thing she had.

"Oh, she wasn't talking to me." He said it without any weight at all, the way you'd correct a date. "She just liked to have said it." He took his hand off the tin and buttoned his coat. Outside, the water had found the second step and was worrying at it.

After he had gone she sat a while with the drives ticking. Then she took the small square from her pocket and played it once more without the headphones, holding the recorder up so the sound came thin into the room. It didn't sound like a warning now. It sounded like permission.

She wrote the card. Owner, device, date, duration; in the last column, *unsent*. Under recipient she drew a short line and left it empty. She put the card in the box and set the little recorder on the shelf beside the whale and the answering machine. On Friday she plugged in the drive and sent the catalogue up the line. It took eleven minutes. When the bar reached the end the fan went quiet and the room was as it had been. Her own memo stayed on her phone. She did not delete it. She did not send it.

Before she locked up she wiped the seam of the little recorder with the toothbrush and emptied the dehumidifier's bucket into the car park, where the tide had been. She walked home with an empty coat pocket. By morning there would be a fine white line along the seam again; there was a fine white line along everything by morning, on the caddies, the window latch, the rim of the jam jar. She would take the toothbrush to it, as she did every morning, with the window open to the water.

# Salt Bloom

The salt came back overnight. It always did. Nell took the phone from the biscuit tin, turned it until the light caught the charging port, and worked a wooden toothpick along the seam. A white crust gave way in grits onto the tray. For the bloom across the case she used a toothbrush gone soft with use. Three phones and a dictaphone waited in the tin, each with masking tape and a number. Nineteen had been the worst: the crystals crunched as the connector went in, a sound like a biscuit breaking.

The council had issued her a dehumidifier rated for a room half this size, which she supposed was forward planning.

It had been the library reading room. Now the shelves held card boxes and labelled drives, and the radiator had gone for the dehumidifier's tube, which ran through the skirting into a bucket. Through the tall windows she could read the numbers painted on the kerbs — 12, 14, 16 — put there for the crews. The houses behind them were empty. The vans had stopped in September.

The council called it the Record of Leaving. The brief said *oral materials of the retiring community*. In practice people handed her devices: old phones, an answering machine, a child's recorder shaped like a whale. Buried among the photographs were memos recorded and never sent. Drafts. She catalogued them on cards — owner, device, date, duration — and in the last column wrote *unsent*. She had written it two hundred and eleven times.

A man from Fennel Lane had recorded an apology to his brother seven times, each shorter than the last; the seventh was four seconds and a click. A woman had sung two lines to a daughter who had not come to the door in six years, then said "No," and stopped the file. Nell never trimmed the silence at the end. It seemed the truest part, the seconds after a person had decided not to say any more.

Salt kept things and salt ate things, and she had never separated the two. It drew the damp out of a board and left a white map across the contacts; it fogged a screen until a face looked out through gauze; it made a tidemark along the rim of the caddies. Every morning she cleaned what she had cleaned the day before. In the afternoons the drives ticked like something cooling.

One device had no number. It had been on the desk the first morning, before she was given the key: a small silver recorder in a padded envelope, no note, the flap tacky with damp. She had written *22* on a strip of tape, put it at the bottom of the tin, and kept not reaching it.

When she finally connected it, the port was clean — the only clean one she had had — and the file came across with its metadata intact. The date field read 04.11.36. Her log lay open at 04.11.26. She checked the recorder, then the wall calendar, then the phone in her pocket, though none had anything to do with that number. The waveform was nine seconds. She put the headphones on.

"Don't send it," her own voice said. Then a breath, and the catch at the back of the throat she had heard all her life on the few recordings anyone had made of her. "It was never for anyone."

The voice was hers, gone slightly rough, the vowels worn narrow the way voices do when used less. Ten years of it sat between the two sentences. She took off the headphones. The room went on ticking.

She played it four times. Between the third and the fourth she wiped the contacts of a phone already cleaned, though there was nothing on them. She did not write a card. She copied it onto a drive of its own and carried it in her coat pocket, a hard square against her hip all afternoon.

On her own phone there was a memo eleven seconds long, recorded six times, never sent and never deleted. Her sister rang on Sunday evenings from the new estate above the bypass, and they talked about the roof, the road, the forms. Afterwards Nell would open the memo, listen to the first second, and close it. She set the phone face down.

By the end of the week she had decided, without deciding, that it was a warning. There was a last transfer on Friday: the whole catalogue going up the line before the exchange closed. She had the upload queued and kept finding reasons not to plug the drive in. It sounded like somebody ten years older who knew how it turned out and had called back to save her the trouble — who knew that no one would ever open the files, that two hundred and eleven people saying nothing to nobody had been a waste of a winter. She heard it in the dehumidifier's click, in the pause before the kettle boiled.

Number 14 had kept its curtains. On Thursday Mr. Coyle came in with a biscuit tin of his own and set it on the desk, keeping his hand on the lid. "She made them after I'd gone up," he said. "I could hear her from the front room. Never loud." He looked at the rack of drives. "Will they go to anyone?"

"They'll be kept," Nell said. It was the only true thing she had.

"Oh, she wasn't talking to me." He said it without any weight, the way you'd correct a date. "She just liked to have said it." He buttoned his coat. Outside, the water had found the second step and was worrying at it.

After he had gone she sat a while with the drives ticking. Then she took the square from her pocket and played it once more without the headphones, holding the recorder up so the sound came thin into the room. It didn't sound like a warning now. It sounded like permission.

She wrote the card. Owner, device, date, duration; in the last column, *unsent*. Under recipient she drew a short line and left it empty. She set the recorder on the shelf beside the whale. On Friday she sent the catalogue up the line. It took eleven minutes. When the bar reached the end the fan went quiet and the room was as it had been. Her own memo stayed on her phone. She did not delete it. She did not send it.

Before she locked up she wiped the seam of the little recorder and emptied the bucket into the car park, where the tide had been. She walked home with an empty coat pocket. By morning there would be a fine white line along the seam again; there was a fine white line along everything by morning, on the caddies, the window latch, the rim of the jar. She would take the toothbrush to it, as she did every morning, with the window open to the water.
